claims.text: HfNbTaTiZr's unusual thermoelastic and stress–strain behavior is governed by thermal-mismatch stresses associated with nanoscale precipitates.
Nanoscale precipitates form in HfNbTaTiZr during aging.
The precipitates have a coefficient of thermal expansion different from that of the surrounding solid-solution matrix.
Differential thermal expansion during cooling or thermal cycling produces internal stresses at precipitate–matrix interfaces.
Precipitate-associated internal stresses alter dislocation nucleation and mobility.
Changes in dislocation behavior caused by mismatch stresses alter creep resistance, cold-work hardening, and elastic response.
The proposed initial HfNbTaTiZr material is a homogeneous alloy with minimal precipitate formation.
Aging HfNbTaTiZr at 600–800 °C promotes nanoscale precipitate formation.
Rapid quenching suppresses precipitate formation relative to aging at 600–800 °C.
Thermal cycling accentuates stresses generated by thermal-expansion mismatch.
Relative to a low-precipitate baseline, the aged material may show higher yield stress at approximately 1250 °C.
Relative to the baseline, the aged material may show increased tertiary creep because of stress concentrations.
The precipitate-rich material should exhibit more pronounced microhardness variation during cold deformation than the low-precipitate baseline.
The precipitate-rich material should exhibit shifted elastic-modulus trends between 293 K and 1100 K relative to the baseline.
Mismatch-related effects are expected to be most significant during aging at 600–800 °C, tensile testing at 1250 °C, and elastic measurements between 293 K and 1100 K.
Outside the specified temperature regimes, solid-solution strengthening or other mechanisms may dominate.

If samples with clearly different precipitate contents and mismatch stresses have statistically indistinguishable creep, hardness, and elastic-modulus responses, the mismatch-stress hypothesis is falsified.
